title: Andal
hook: Andal questions a conch shell: does his mouth smell of camphor, or of the lotus?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andal, and the offering a jackal sniffed: her picture of any match but the Lord. Did you keep one small thing set apart? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

Does it smell of camphor? Of the lotus flower? Is it sweet? A young woman is asking these questions, urgently, and she's asking them of a seashell. Not any shell. The white conch that rests in the hand of Vishnu, and that Krishna lifts to his lips and blows. She wants to know what his mouth is like, and the conch is the only one who'd know. It's Andal again, in the seventh song of the Nachiyar Tirumoli, and she's jealous of a shell.
screen: `CAMPHOR? THE LOTUS? IS IT SWEET?` → `THE WHITE CONCH.` → `JEALOUS OF A SHELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening, in paraphrase. Does it smell of camphor, does it smell of the lotus, does his coral mouth taste sweet? I long to know. Tell me, white conch of the deep sea, what is the scent and taste of the lips of the one who broke the elephant's tusk? Then the song keeps going, and the questions turn into complaints. You were born in the ocean, she tells the conch, and now you live in his hand. You rest on his mouth while the rest of us wait. Others can only stand and look at him from afar, and you, a shell, get to go right up to his lips. It's a love poem, and a funny one, in a way. She's talking to an object, and she's envious of it. So why a conch? In the Bhagavad Gita, before the battle, Krishna blows his conch, named Panchajanya. For a Vaishnava listener, the conch in the poem isn't decoration. It's one of the Lord's own emblems, held in his hand, carrying his breath. There's a second layer. Sri Vaishnava teachers read the conch as a picture of the devotee the Lord keeps nearest, close enough to carry his breath. So Andal's envy is also a wish: let me be that close, let my life be the instrument his breath moves through. And a third. This is temple scripture, recited by priests and families, and it's full of taste and scent and lips and jealousy. The tradition didn't clean it up. It kept a young woman's desire, plain and bodily, as a way of talking about God.
screen: `QUESTIONS FOR A SEASHELL` · `ENVY OF THE ONE AT HIS LIPS` · `THE CONCH IN KRISHNA'S HAND` · `DESIRE KEPT AS SCRIPTURE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the breath through the instrument. Sit, and let the breath come and go on its own. Notice how it moves through you, the way breath moves through a conch to make a sound. Feel the air at the nose, the chest rising, the long breath out. You don't have to make any sound. Just let yourself be the shell the breath passes through. If you pray, you can let one breath out carry a name you love. The bell holds the time.
Andal. In the Nachiyar Tirumoli she questions Vishnu's white conch about his lips, and envies the shell for being so close to him. Today's word.
Your line: Andal. Today, notice one ordinary object that gets close to someone you love, a cup or a pen or a scarf, and let it remind you of her conch. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Sri Vaishnava Hindus recite Andal's Nachiyar Tirumoli in temples and homes, and in Vishnu worship the conch is blown and held as one of the Lord's own emblems.

notes: Nachiyar Tirumoli 7.1 ('karpuram narumo, kamalappu narumo'): confirm the paraphrase, including 'coral mouth', 'white conch of the deep sea' and the epithet for Krishna who broke the elephant's tusk (Kuvalayapida).
Nachiyar Tirumoli 7 (later verses): confirm the complaints that the conch was born in the ocean and now rests in his hand and at his mouth while others only look on.
The reading of the conch as the devotee kept nearest is given as Sri Vaishnava teachers' reading; check against the commentarial tradition.
howItsDone: confirm the wording about the conch in Vishnu worship.
